mcqs.question: Per the spectrum in this topic, when does Svelte determine a component's reactive dependencies?
options: At compile time, before the app even runs, via static analysis of the source
At runtime, once, during component setup
At runtime, on every single render
Only when a developer explicitly calls a subscribe function
mcqs.explanation: Svelte's compiler analyzes the component ahead of time and emits targeted update instructions directly — the analysis happens once, at build time, unlike Vue's runtime-but-once tracking or React's every-render rediscovery.

mcqs.question: Why can a small Svelte app ship a meaningfully smaller bundle than an equivalent React app?
options: Because Svelte components are not allowed to use conditional rendering
Because much of the reactivity work is baked into compiled, component-specific code rather than shipped as a general-purpose runtime
Because Svelte does not support component composition
Because React requires a virtual DOM library that Vue and Svelte both lack entirely
mcqs.explanation: Svelte's compiler generates the exact update code each component needs, so there's no generic diffing runtime to ship to the browser — React ships that runtime because it discovers dependencies at runtime instead. Svelte fully supports composition and conditionals; Vue does keep a virtual DOM, it's Svelte that lacks one.

mcqs.question: What's true about React's JSX, Vue's templates, and Svelte's compiled templates, despite their different syntax?
options: Only JSX supports arbitrary JavaScript expressions inside markup
Vue's templates compile to the exact same runtime API calls as JSX
All three ultimately produce instructions for building and updating a DOM tree
Svelte's templates cannot express conditional rendering or loops
mcqs.explanation: Despite very different authoring syntax, all three compile down to the same underlying job — describing how to build and update the DOM. Svelte handles loops and conditionals natively (`{#each}`, `{#if}`); Vue's directives are a constrained subset of JS, not identical compiled output to JSX.

mcqs.question: Why is a plain `let` variable reactive inside a Svelte component with no special wrapper, unlike React's `useState`?
options: Because Svelte components cannot hold any state at all
Because Svelte automatically converts every variable in the entire application into global state
Because Svelte requires an explicit `reactive()` call around every variable, the same as Vue
Because reactivity in Svelte is a compiler feature — the compiler detects and instruments variable reassignment directly, with no runtime wrapper needed
mcqs.explanation: The compiler statically rewrites assignments to component-level variables into the update code needed, so there's no `ref()`-style wrapper required — this follows directly from reactivity being a compile-time feature rather than a runtime API, unlike both React's `useState` and Vue's `ref`.

mcqs.question: What's the mistake in saying "Svelte is faster because it doesn't use JSX"?
options: It attributes a performance difference to syntax, when the actual cause is the compile-time reactivity model underneath, which happens to pair with different syntax but isn't caused by it
Svelte does in fact use JSX, so the premise is factually wrong
Performance differences between frameworks are entirely determined by bundle size, not syntax or reactivity
JSX is objectively slower than any HTML-like template syntax in every framework
mcqs.explanation: Syntax is the most visible but least consequential difference between frameworks — the actual driver is when and how dependency tracking happens, not what the markup looks like. Svelte genuinely doesn't use JSX, but that fact isn't the mechanism behind its performance characteristics.
